title: API 653 Training in Corpus Christi: Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: API 653 tank inspector exam prep for Corpus Christi and Ingleside terminal, refinery and tank crews: self-paced online study with instructor Q&A.
h1: API 653 Training in Corpus Christi, TX: Aboveground Storage Tank Inspector Exam Prep for Export Terminals and Tank Farms
html:
API 653 exam prep for Corpus Christi tank inspectors

The Port of Corpus Christi describes itself as the number one US gateway for crude oil exports, and behind every cargo is a tank. Crude arriving from the Permian Basin and the Eagle Ford is stored at Ingleside and around the Inner Harbor before it is loaded onto tankers; refineries on the ship channel keep their own farms of crude, intermediate and product tanks; chemical plants on both sides of the bay store feedstocks and finished products. All of those atmospheric tanks need inspection, repair approvals and settlement and thickness evaluations, and API 653 is the certification for the inspectors who carry that responsibility.

This page is for terminal technicians, NDT crews, tank construction hands, operators and engineers on the Coastal Bend who are preparing for the API 653 Aboveground Storage Tank Inspector examination. Atlantis NDT's course is self-paced and online, with an instructor answering your questions while you study. There is no Atlantis classroom in Corpus Christi or anywhere else. The American Petroleum Institute determines eligibility under Annex D of API 653, administers the examination in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification; you apply to API yourself, and Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider.

The tank farms of Corpus Christi Bay and Ingleside

Published figures from the operators give a sense of the scale a local API 653 inspector works at.

Terminal or tank farmOperatorWhat the operator or a public source reports
Enbridge Ingleside Energy CenterEnbridgeAbout 20 million barrels of storage after its Phase VII tank expansion added 2.5 million; four deep-water berths, two able to load VLCCs; loadings in 2025 averaging about 1.13 million barrels a day; direct connections to the Gray Oak, Cactus I, Cactus II, EPIC and Harvest pipelines
South Texas Gateway Terminal, InglesideGibson Energy, which completed its purchase from Buckeye Partners, Phillips 66 and Marathon Petroleum in 20238.6 million barrels across 20 tanks after an expansion completed in early 2021; VLCC capability and direct pipeline links to the Permian and Eagle Ford
Flint Hills Resources Ingleside terminalFlint Hills ResourcesFlint Hills says it sold the terminal's marine docks to Enbridge and kept ownership of the crude oil terminal
Refinery tank farms on the Corpus Christi Ship ChannelValero; Flint Hills Resources; other refinersCrude, intermediate and product storage supporting refineries EIA lists at 290,000 barrels per calendar day (Valero) and 290,000 plus 87,500 (Flint Hills West and East)
Public and private oil docksPort of Corpus Christi and port industriesThe port says it owns and operates 13 public oil docks, and port industries operate 16 private ones

Two other kinds of storage complete the local picture. Chemical and petrochemical sites, such as the ExxonMobil and SABIC complex in San Patricio County and OxyChem's site near Corpus Christi, keep tanks of feedstock and product that may or may not be API 650 construction. And Cheniere's liquefaction terminal stores LNG in large refrigerated tanks. API 653 is written for steel tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor API 12C, so the refrigerated LNG tanks and shop-fabricated tanks built to other standards sit outside it; knowing what a tank was built to is the first question an inspector asks.

The rules that put an API 653 inspector on a Coastal Bend tank

Three regulatory routes lead to the same certification here, and the exam's terminology makes more sense once you know which one applies to the tank you are standing beside.

EPA's SPCC rule

Under 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6), facilities covered by the Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure rule must test or inspect each aboveground container for integrity on a regular schedule and whenever material repairs are made, following industry standards. EPA's fact sheet names API 653 as the standard typically used for field-erected tanks and STI SP001 for shop-fabricated ones. If a facility's plan says it follows API 653, the relevant parts of the standard become mandatory, and the formal external and internal inspections it calls for are carried out by an API 653 certified inspector. Inspection records must be kept for three years, and EPA recommends keeping formal reports for the life of the tank. See who can inspect tanks under SPCC and STI SP001 versus API 653.

PHMSA's breakout tank rule

Tanks that relieve surges on a hazardous liquid pipeline, or that receive and store liquid for reinjection into one, are breakout tanks, and 49 CFR 195.432 has operators inspect them in accordance with API 653. That rule does not allow API 653's risk-based option to set the internal inspection interval. Whether a given terminal tank is a breakout tank depends on how it is used, so on a coast where several long-haul crude lines end, classification comes before any interval is set.

PSM mechanical integrity

Where a tank is part of a process covered by OSHA's Process Safety Management standard, the mechanical integrity paragraph lists storage tanks among the equipment that must be inspected and tested to recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and owners commonly name API 653 as that practice.

What export service does to tank floors, roofs and shells

A tank at a busy export terminal lives a harder life than a slow-turning refinery tank, and the API 653 code and its companion documents read differently once you have seen why.

  • Floors. Water and sediment drop out of crude between transfers and sit on the bottom, where product-side pitting starts. Soil-side corrosion depends on the foundation, drainage and cathodic protection, which is why API RP 651 is in the Body of Knowledge; internal linings, covered by RP 652, are a common answer to product-side attack. The guide to tank floor pitting and minimum remaining thickness works through the floor calculation.
  • Floating roofs. Crude tanks at export terminals are commonly floating-roof tanks, and frequent fills and draws move the roof through its full travel again and again. Seals, roof drains, pontoons and supports wear accordingly; see floating roof inspection.
  • Shells. Salt-laden onshore wind attacks external coatings, especially near the water, and wind girders and stairways corrode at crevices. Shell thickness is judged against the API 653 minimums.
  • Foundations. Coastal soils settle, and heavy rain or storm surge can undermine a ringwall or wash out a foundation. Annex B's settlement evaluation is a regular exam topic for that reason, and a hurricane season running from June through November gives local inspectors plenty of post-storm surveys.
  • Release prevention. Leak detection and containment under the bottom change both the minimum floor thickness and the maximum internal interval; see release prevention barriers.

A worked shell interval for a terminal tank

API 653 sets two shell-related intervals from the same pair of numbers: RCA, the remaining corrosion allowance (measured thickness minus minimum required thickness, in mils), and N, the shell corrosion rate in mils per year.

On a crude tank at an Ingleside-style terminal, the thinnest reading on the bottom course is 0.480 in. and the minimum required thickness for that course is 0.380 in. The shell corrosion rate from past surveys is 0.004 in. per year.

  • RCA = 480 − 380 = 100 mils; N = 4 mils per year.
  • Ultrasonic thickness interval, with the rate known: the smaller of RCA/2N and 15 years. RCA/2N = 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5 years, so 12.5 years.
  • External inspection by an authorized inspector: the lesser of 5 years and RCA/4N. RCA/4N = 100 ÷ 16 = 6.25 years, so the 5-year ceiling governs.

Now double the corrosion rate to 8 mils per year, as might happen after coating breakdown on the windward side. RCA/2N becomes 6.25 years and RCA/4N becomes 3.1 years, so the external inspection interval drops below five years. The traps are the units, since mixing inches and mils gives answers a thousand times out, and forgetting that the 5-year and 15-year ceilings still apply. Had the corrosion rate been unknown, the maximum UT interval would have been 5 years. The national API 653 certification page and the API 653 tank inspection guide put these intervals in context.

Studying API 653 around terminal operations

Terminals run around the clock, so tank people on the Coastal Bend often work rotating shifts, and out-of-service inspections bunch up whenever tanks are cleaned for inspection or repair. That pattern suits self-paced study. Some suggestions from the way the course is organised:

  1. Study API 650 alongside API 653 from the start. The open-book questions keep sending you from API 653 into API 650 for allowable stresses, weld details and new-construction requirements, and the cross-references are easy to lose under time pressure.
  2. Use every tank opened for inspection as a study aid. When you see a bottom being scanned, a shell being gauged or a roof being repaired, look up the paragraph that governs it afterwards.
  3. Read API RP 575 for the inspection practice behind the code, and RP 651 and RP 652 for the corrosion control questions the exam draws from them.
  4. Leave room around storm season and around big out-of-service campaigns when you pick your window, and use the instructor Q&A for clauses that read two ways.

Eligibility routes into API 653 for Coastal Bend workers

API sets API 653 eligibility through Annex D of the standard: education plus experience in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of aboveground storage tanks, gained within the last ten years, and every route includes at least one year supervising or performing tank inspection. The API 653 certification requirements page has the full table. Locally:

  • Tank construction crews. The terminal expansions at Ingleside have meant years of new tank building. That construction experience counts on the two-year-degree, high school and no-formal-education routes, but candidates still need a year of inspection work.
  • Floor scanning and UT technicians. NDT technicians who scan floors and gauge shells during out-of-service inspections are building inspection experience directly; ASNT training for that work is described on NDT training in Corpus Christi.
  • Terminal operators. Operating experience counts toward the longer routes; the inspection year is usually the part to plan for.
  • Engineers. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology needs one year of supervising or performing tank inspection.

Choosing how to prepare for API 653 in Corpus Christi

Local candidates usually choose between mentoring from an experienced tank inspector at their own employer, fixed-date classroom courses run by other providers in larger cities, self-study from the code books, and self-paced online preparation. Mentoring is the best source of field judgement but rarely covers the whole Body of Knowledge; classroom courses bring structure but mean travel and time away from the roster; self-study costs least but makes the open-book technique hard to practise. The Atlantis course covers the publications on your window's effectivity sheet, worked calculations and timed papers, with an instructor to ask, and it works alongside an employer's mentoring.

Sponsoring tank inspectors from a Corpus Christi terminal or refinery

Terminal operators and inspection contractors often prepare two or three people at once, for example a lead technician and an engineer, ahead of a busy out-of-service campaign. A group enquiry can mix API 653 with API 510 or 570 candidates, and fees are quoted on request. Every tank inspector in the group files a separate API application, keeps their own pace through the material and raises their own questions with the instructor. For NDE support on tanks rather than training, see tank inspection services in Corpus Christi.

faq.q: Does my terminal's SPCC plan mean it needs an API 653 certified inspector?
faq.a: If the plan states that the facility follows API 653 for its field-erected tanks, EPA treats the relevant parts of the standard as mandatory, and API 653's formal external and internal inspections are carried out by an API 653 certified inspector. Routine walk-around checks can usually be done by trained facility staff. Shop-built tanks are often inspected to STI SP001 instead. Check what your own plan says.

faq.q: Are pipeline breakout tanks on the Coastal Bend inspected differently from refinery tanks?
faq.a: They are inspected to API 653 under PHMSA's rule at 49 CFR 195.432, which does not let the risk-based option in API 653 set their internal inspection interval. A refinery tank outside that rule can use the risk-based route if its owner meets the standard's conditions. For an API 653 candidate the code is the same; what differs is which interval options the regulation allows.

faq.q: Do the LNG tanks at Corpus Christi Liquefaction count as API 653 experience?
faq.a: Generally not as tank inspection under API 653, because those refrigerated tanks are built to other standards and fall outside API 653's scope, which covers steel tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor API 12C. Inspection experience on atmospheric tanks at the same site, if there are any, is another matter. API decides what counts, so describe the tanks and the work precisely.

faq.q: Can tank construction work on a new Ingleside tank count toward API 653 eligibility?
faq.a: Yes, on the routes that accept construction experience: the two-year degree or certificate, high school and no-formal-education lines all count design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of tanks. Each of those routes also requires at least one year supervising or performing tank inspection, so a construction hand usually needs to move into inspection work before applying. Only experience from the last ten years counts.

faq.q: Is the API 653 exam open book, and do I need API 650 as well?
faq.a: The exam has a closed-book part and an open-book part, and in the open-book part the code PDFs are on the computer, API 650 among them. You need API 650 because API 653 refers to it for allowable stresses, construction details and reconstruction. Practise moving between the two documents in PDF form, since that is where most time is lost on the day.

faq.q: Is there a Corpus Christi classroom for API 653 exam prep?
faq.a: No. The Atlantis course is studied online at your own pace, with instructor Q&A, so a terminal technician on nights and an engineer in the city follow the same material. You can start when you enrol. The examination itself is taken in person at a Prometric test centre after API has accepted your application, and Prometric lists centres in and around Corpus Christi.

faq.q: Can a terminal operator enrol its tank team as a group?
faq.a: Yes. Operators and contractors often sponsor several candidates together, and a group can include people preparing for API 510 or API 570 as well as API 653. Fees are quoted on request. Each person studies individually at their own pace, asks the instructor their own questions and submits their own application to API, with the employer confirming their experience.
